newsitem.title: LUXEMBOURG: UK'S Brown backs French delay on stability pact.
newsitem.headline: UK'S Brown backs French delay on stability pact.

text.p: Britain's Chancellor of the Exchequer Gordon Brown on Monday backed France's decision to delay signing the stability pact for monetary union and said he and the French finance minister agreed jobs were the European Union's top priority.
Brown was speaking after delivering a plan on job creation to European Union finance ministers gathered here for their monthly meeting.

Britain's Labour government is hoping to establish itself at the helm of the EU with policies focused on economic recovery rather than the single currency timetable. But on Monday, new French finance minister Dominique Strauss-Kahn stole the show.

He told his EU counterparts France could not sign the stability pact as expected next Monday at the Amsterdam summit of European leaders because it would not give the government enough time to consult the new parliament.

He asked for time to study the framework which will impose fines on countries who fail to keep their budget deficits under control once a single European currency gets underway. It would take more than a week to do that, Strauss-Kahn said, sending Europe's markets into turmoil in the process.

Brown said he supported France's decision. "France wants to take time to make representations to its National Assembly...and it is right for them to do that first," he told Reuters Financial Television. "It wants to present proposals to the National Assembly first, then the European Community."

EU leaders agreed on the terms of the stability pact at last December's Dublin summit. The pact incorporates automatic fines for countries whose budget deficits exceed 3.0 percent of GDP, unless they are in recession.

Members of France's new Socialist government, elected just a week ago, have said they are unhappy that the pact, officially called the Growth and Stability pact, is too heavily weighted in favour of price stability at the cost of growth and jobs.
The pact was due to be ratified at the Amsterdam summit but now looks set to be delayed until at least the end of June to allow France time to consult parliament.
Brown said he and Strauss-Kahn had held bilateral talks and agreed that jobs were the key issue in Europe.
"Mr Strauss-Kahn and I were in complete agreement about the central importance of jobs, about the need to look at new initiatives both at a European level and a national level," he told reporters.

But Britain's Chancellor stopped short of sympathising with French concerns over growth, reasserting his own fiscal credentials. "Budget discipline is absolutely critical, so is price stability. But I don't see an inbuilt contradiction between achieving these two aims and achieving the job creation growth we want to see."
Brown's employment proposal has three main strands -- job creation and employability, help for small businesses to create jobs and completing the EU single market.
He said his initiative, circulated on Sunday night and discussed over lunch on Monday, had been well received.
"I found it was generally supported. Jobs and growth are central to the European Union's agenda and ministers across the political spectrum welcomed it," he said.

While the plan leans towards free market policies, it does not amount to a hard sell of the virtues of Britain's flexible and deregulated jobs market. It said as well as promoting economic growth and stability, governments must invest in human capital and create a fair and inclusive society.

Brown said the time had come to move on from the EU obsession with the timetable for economic and monetary union. Employment was more important than who was going to join in the first round of monetary union in 1999.

"In or out of monetary union, people in Europe now know that unless we face up to the issue of jobs and low growth, Europe will remain sluggish and we will not create the prosperity that everyone wants," he told the BBC.
